summary: The paper proposes LayerBudget, a training-free online heuristic that jointly allocates a per-layer KV-cache token budget n_l and quantization bit-width b_l in {4,8,16} under a global memory budget, by greedy marginal-gain (Delta Q / Delta M) selection over a factorized quality model Q = C(l,n_l) * F(b_l) * w_l (coverage power law from an attention Gini coefficient, cosine-similarity fidelity, sigmoid depth importance). Two auxiliary tricks are added: 'inverted' importance (protect early layers) and mean-fill of evicted KV slots. Evaluation covers 7 models (7B-72B, MHA and GQA), 17 self-reimplemented baselines, WikiText-2 PPL ratio at 1024 tokens plus 16K/32K, MMLU, GSM8K, NIAH, LongBench-v1, one RULER column, and a vLLM block-manager port. I reviewed this as the venue reviewer, i.e. asking whether it is written for, positioned against, and evaluated by the standards of the top-tier efficient-inference community. My verdict is that the contribution IS statable in this community's vocabulary (so it is not mis-venued in the linguistic sense), but the paper fails this venue on three independent counts. (1) Positioning: the related work engages a set of 2024-2026 arXiv preprints and completely omits this venue's own recent accepted literature on the exact problem (STAR-KV ICML'26 Spotlight, KVTC ICLR'26, DefensiveKV / Layer-DefensiveKV ICLR'26, TurboQuant ICLR'26, HqeKV ACL'26 Findings, RDKV, ThinKV), several of which operate at 14-20x compression or <5% cache retention while this paper's envelope is 2-4x and already breaks at 6x. (2) Evaluation conventions: the primary metric is WikiText-2 PPL ratio, a proxy this community has largely retired for KV compression precisely because quantization trivially preserves it (the paper's own KIVI row is flat at 1.01 across every CR); LongBench-v2, InfiniteBench, SCBench, HELMET, effective-bits/token, and the KVPress harness are all absent, the query-aware vs query-agnostic compression order is never stated, and the reported LongBench-v1 scores (Full KV = 0.040-0.056) are two orders of magnitude below the normal scale of that benchmark, i.e. the harness is broken. (3) The fatal-flaw gate fires on the science itself: the paper's own component ablation shows the joint allocator never beats quantization-only (tie at 3x on both 7B models; 3.23 vs 1.00 and 45.09 vs 1.01 at 6x), KIVI ties or beats LayerBudget on PPL, MMLU, LongBench, 32K PPL, and at 72B on PPL/NIAH/RULER, and the paper's own memory table has KIVI at 9,990 KB / 1.01 versus LayerBudget at 12,939 KB / 1.07 -- fewer bytes AND better quality. The abstract's 'ranks first' is preserved only by scoping the comparison to 'token-compression methods', which excludes the baseline that wins. Independently, I found arithmetic that does not survive recomputation: the fidelity constant Delta F(4->8) = 0.0035 used in the concavity argument is 6.4x smaller than the 0.0224 implied by the paper's own calibration table; the memory-savings table reports Base KV of 189 MB for Llama-3.1-8B and 95 MB for Mistral-7B at 512 tokens although the two models have identical KV geometry (32L, 8 KV heads, d=128), so the headline '43-72% savings' range is an artifact and collapses to ~43% once corrected; and none of the three rows in that CR=2x table actually delivers 50% savings, contradicting the Byte-CR appendix's claim that effective CR matches nominal CR within +/-0.05. The source also contains compile-breaking LaTeX and an 18-column table wrapped in \resizebox, which the NeurIPS handbook names as a desk-reject trigger. This is a large, honest, hard-working empirical study that is aimed at the wrong bar and, on its own numbers, is dominated by INT4 quantization in the only regime it claims to win.
strengths: The unified reimplementation of 17 baselines behind one interface with a single explicitly-stated CR denominator (Section 4, 'Compression ratio (CR) definition') is the paper's genuine asset, and the due diligence around it is above average for this literature: the MMLU table's caption reports that the H2O collapse was re-verified against a faithful per-head reimplementation matching the official FMInference/H2O algorithm (recent_ratio=0.1, per-head heavy-hitter selection) and still gives 29.4%, and the xKV appendix states the exact byte accounting used (r*(S + n_h*d) = S*n_h*d/CR per group) rather than hand-waving it. Most KV-compression submissions do neither.

The paper reports its own failures in a form a reviewer can audit rather than burying them: MiniKV's 11.92 PPL ratio on Mistral at 6x is footnoted as 'the measured ratio (not a typo)'; Limitation (5) concedes that shared-b_l is dominated by MoE-nD's independent (b_K, b_V) at 6x (1.25 vs 1.04); the LayerBudget-KV appendix concedes the variant's 4K NIAH drops to 26.7%; and the Byte-CR Reconciliation appendix openly documents a 2x discrepancy between allocator-side and runtime memory accounting. This candor is why I was able to run the recomputations below at all, and it deserves explicit credit even though (per the calibration instructions) it does not offset the underlying defects.

Model and regime breadth exceeds the norm for this area: 7 models spanning 7B-72B and both MHA (Llama-2-7B/13B) and GQA (Mistral, Llama-3.1, Qwen3-8B, Qwen2.5-14B/72B), a 16K/32K long-context table, and head-to-head reimplementations of two concurrent methods (MoE-nD, xKV) rather than only citing them. The 72B point in particular is a real cost that few groups pay.

The online-ness of the signal is a defensible differentiator and is argued correctly: the Gini statistic is computed from the last attention row only, O(S) per layer instead of O(S^2) (Section 3.3), so unlike the offline-calibrated concurrent work (KVTuner, MoE-nD, PolyKV, ARKV) the allocation can in principle be made per-request. The positioning table in Appendix B is the right way to make that argument.

Mean-fill is a cheap, portable idea with the correct control experiment attached: the paper measures logits KL (0.249 -> 0.009 on Mistral, 0.6696 -> 0.0636 on Llama-2-7B) rather than only end metrics, gives a first-moment-preservation mechanism, and then reports that median-fill and moment-matched random-fill do just as well -- which is the honest control that shows the effect is 'do not zero-fill', not 'use the mean'.
weaknesses: [FATAL, gate (a)] The method ties or loses to the fairest and simplest strong baseline -- pure INT4 quantization -- on essentially every metric that matters, by the paper's own numbers. Component analysis (Appendix table A1): at 3x, Joint = Quant-only exactly (Mistral 1.00 vs 1.00; Llama-2 1.02 vs 1.02); at 6x, Joint is catastrophically worse (Mistral 3.23 vs 1.00; Llama-2 45.09 vs 1.01). Main table: KIVI is 1.01-1.02 flat while LayerBudget is 1.00-1.03 at 2-4x and 1.03-1.25 at 6x. At 32K on Mistral, KIVI 1.008 vs LB 1.009. At 72B, KIVI matches or beats LB on PPL (1.00 vs 1.06 at 6x), NIAH (100/100 both) and RULER (99/100 vs 98/100). MMLU: LB vs KIVI is 47.7/47.7, 64.1/63.7, 60.1/60.1, 72.6/72.7, 76.1/76.6 -- every gap far inside the +/-1.45pp standard error of 1140 questions. The memory-vs-quality table has KIVI at 9,990 KB with PPL 1.01 against LayerBudget at 12,939 KB with PPL 1.07: fewer bytes and better quality. The abstract survives this only by scoping to 'token-compression methods', i.e. by excluding the baseline that wins. The single surviving differentiator is NIAH on Llama-2-7B (100 vs 93.3) and Mistral 2x (86.7 vs 73.3); with 10 depths x 3 needles = 30 cells (stated in Appendix C), 93.3% is 28/30 and 73.3% is 22/30, so these are 2- and 4-question differences with binomial 95% CIs that overlap 100%. Fix: either demonstrate a regime where the joint allocator strictly dominates INT4 quantization at equal bytes with non-overlapping CIs on a retrieval/long-context benchmark of adequate size, or restate the contribution as 'matches quantization while additionally reducing token count', which is a much weaker claim.

[FATAL, gate (b)] The load-bearing importance prior is contradicted by the paper's own measurement on 2 of the 3 architectures it probes, and is nonetheless used for every headline number. Section 3.2 states that Llama-2-13B is late-bottleneck (+0.093 late vs +0.030 early) and Qwen2.5-14B is flat (+0.039 vs +0.038), then says 'we ... report end-to-end results under it across all models for consistency'. So the 13B, 14B and 72B rows in the scaling tables were produced with an importance direction the paper itself shows is wrong for those models, and the visible cost is Llama-2-13B at 1.11 (4x) and 1.56 (6x). Meanwhile the ablation table caption still asserts the universal 'Inverted importance dominates because early layers are most damaged by eviction'. Fix: rerun the 13B/14B/72B end-to-end results under the per-architecture LOO-selected direction the paper recommends, and rewrite that caption.

[P13 - venue positioning] The related work positions against a set of arXiv preprints and omits this venue's own recent accepted work on the identical problem. Missing entirely: STAR-KV (ICML 2026 Spotlight, 20x with low-rank-aware mixed-precision quantization), KVTC (ICLR 2026, 20-40x, global bit budget), DefensiveKV and Layer-DefensiveKV (ICLR 2026, per-layer budget allocation, RULER 91.4 at 20% cache), TurboQuant (ICLR 2026), 'Adaptive KV-Cache Compression without Manually Setting Budget' (ICLR 2026, the same scoring->allocation-> selection formalization), RDKV (rate-distortion joint eviction+quantization, the closest formal framing), HqeKV (ACL 2026 Findings, hybrid quantization+eviction, code public), and ThinKV (hybrid quant+eviction, near-lossless at <5% cache). Layer-DefensiveKV alone is per-layer budget allocation reporting 91.4 RULER at 5x, a regime where this paper is already degrading. A PC member will read 'To our knowledge, no prior online, training-free method jointly optimizes per-layer (n_l, b_l)' against this list and conclude the novelty claim was not checked against the venue's own proceedings. Fix: add these, and state explicitly why 2-4x is a regime worth publishing when accepted work sits at 14-20x.

[P14 / P13 - evaluation conventions] The primary metric is the one this community has retired for KV compression. WikiText-2 PPL ratio at 1024 tokens carries every headline claim, yet the paper's own KIVI row (1.01 flat at 2x/3x/4x/6x) demonstrates why: PPL is insensitive to exactly the failure modes compression causes. LongBench-v2, InfiniteBench, SCBench, HELMET and effective-bits/token are absent; RULER appears in two columns of one 72B table; NIAH is 30 cells at 4096 tokens; GSM8K is 200 samples with Llama-2 Full KV at 5.5% (floor, so that column is uninformative); MMLU is 0-shot at short context, where KV compression is least stressed. The de-facto community harness (NVIDIA KVPress, which ships PerLayerCompressionPress and QuantizedCache) is not used, so 17 hand-reimplemented baselines carry the 'ranks 1st' claim. Fix: report RULER 4K-128K and LongBench-v2 across the model suite under a public harness, and report effective bits/token alongside CR.

[P14 - broken benchmark reported as a positive result] The LongBench table reports Full KV at 0.056 / 0.040 / 0.050 (Mistral / Llama-3.1 / Llama-2-7B) as 'mean F1/ROUGE-L across 16 English tasks'. LongBench F1/ROUGE-L on these models is normally in the 20-45 range; 0.05 means the generation or scoring path is producing essentially nothing. The paper then claims 'LayerBudget matches Full KV on all models' from LB = 0.055 / 0.040 / 0.050 -- a match at the noise floor of a broken harness, and one of the '8 evaluation tasks' the abstract counts. The footnote about H2O's 0.097 being 'degenerate repetition inflating F1' is itself evidence the harness is measuring degenerate output. Fix: debug the LongBench pipeline (prompt truncation and answer extraction are the usual culprits) and re-report, or remove the table.

[P4 - baseline configuration] SnapKV scores 27.1 / 29.6 / 29.4 / 33.4 on MMLU (Llama-2 / Llama-3.1 / Mistral / Qwen3) -- at or below the 25% chance floor for 4-way MMLU on three models -- for a method that is near-lossless at these ratios in its own paper and in every published reproduction. The paper verifies the H2O collapse against the official algorithm but performs no such check for SnapKV. The community has documented the exact mechanism that produces this: SnapKV is a query-aware method whose observation window must see the question, and it collapses below a keep-start-plus-recent trivial baseline when compression is applied query-agnostically. The paper never states which order it uses. Fix: state the compression order (query-aware vs query-agnostic) for every table, and re-verify SnapKV as was done for H2O; the 'ranks 1st among 17 baselines' claim is not credible while a canonical baseline sits at chance.

[P3/P5 - recomputation failure #1] The fidelity constant that drives the allocator's bit-upgrade gain is wrong by 6.4x relative to the paper's own calibration table. Section 3.5 states 'fidelity gains are diminishing (Delta F(4->8) = 0.0035 > Delta F(8->16) = 0.0001)'. The Per-Model Fidelity Calibration table gives mean F(4) = (0.9794+0.9758+0.9817+0.9683+0.9781+0.9810)/6 = 0.97738 and mean F(8) ~ 0.99980, so Delta F(4->8) = 0.02242, not 0.0035 (and Delta F(8->16) = 0.0002, not 0.0001). Section 3.2 independently describes the same gap as '~2%', consistent with 0.0224 and inconsistent with 0.0035. This is not cosmetic: Delta F(4->8) is the numerator of the bit-upgrade marginal gain, so if the implementation used 0.0035 the allocator systematically under-prices exactly the action the paper's central 'quantize first, evict last' principle depends on. Fix: state which value the code uses, and rerun the allocations if it is 0.0035.

[P3/P5 - recomputation failure #2] The memory-savings table is internally impossible and its headline range is an arithmetic artifact. Llama-3.1-8B and Mistral-7B have identical KV geometry (32 layers, 8 KV heads, d=128), so their FP16 KV cache at 512 tokens must be identical: 2*32*512*8*128*2 = 67.1 MB. The table reports 189 MB for Llama-3.1-8B and 95 MB for Mistral-7B -- differing by exactly 1.99x -- while reporting the same 54 MB compressed size for both. Consequently the '71.2% savings' for Llama-3.1 is 54/189 and the '42.9%' for Mistral is 54/95; correcting the base makes both 43%, and the abstract/text claim 'GQA models achieve 43-72% memory savings' collapses to a single number. Fix: recompute Base KV analytically per model and reissue the table and the claim.

[P5 - the CR the paper delivers is not the CR it claims] The same table is captioned 'KV cache memory savings at CR=2x' but reports 24.3%, 71.2% and 42.9% savings, i.e. effective compression of 1.32x, 3.50x and 1.76x. None is 2x. This directly contradicts Appendix E, which audits 1,779 checkpoints and concludes 'every method's effective CR ... matches its nominal CR within +/-0.05'; the deviations here are 0.68, 1.50 and 0.24 -- 5x to 30x the claimed tolerance. Since 'near-lossless at 2-4x' is the paper's central claim, a reader cannot currently tell what compression the quality numbers correspond to. Fix: one memory denominator (mean_memory_bytes) for every table, and a per-row effective-CR column.

[P5/P12 - the headline envelope is measured in a mode the paper itself calls non-deployment] All main-table numbers use mean-fill, but Section 4.3 calls zero-fill 'the practical deployment setting'. Section 4.3 then claims 'Under zero-fill evaluation ... LayerBudget achieves ratio <=1.04 at 2-4x on all tested models', which its own appendix table contradicts: Llama-2-7B zero-fill is 1.17 at 4x and 45.09 at 6x, and Mistral is 3.23 at 6x. So the abstract's '<=1.03 at 4x' describes the non-deployment evaluation mode. Fix: report both fills for every headline cell, and correct the '<=1.04' sentence.

[P5 - abstract contradicts the results tables] The abstract states 'PPL ratio <=1.03 at 4x on seven models from 7B to 72B'. The large-model table gives Llama-2-13B at 1.11 at 4x. The abstract's own follow-on clause ('1.00-1.03 on the 7B suite, <=1.01 on 13B-72B at GQA') is worded to exclude the 13B MHA model, so the sentence contradicts itself within one line. Separately, Llama-2-7B at 6x appears as 1.099 in the head-to-head table and 1.17 in the main table, both stated as seq=1024, mean-fill; and KIVI on Llama-2-7B is 1.006 in one and 1.02 in the other. Fix: reconcile or annotate the differing configurations.

[P3/P11 - the allocator cost projection is off by ~160x] Section 3.4 argues Qwen2.5-72B at S=32K needs 80*32768/8 = 327,680 iterations and '~10 ms' at 30 ns each (327,680 * 30 ns = 9.83 ms, which checks out internally). But Algorithm 1's WHILE body contains a FOR over every layer and both actions, so each outer iteration costs O(L) marginal-gain evaluations: 327,680 * 80 * 2 = 52.4M evaluations, ~1.6 s at 30 ns, not 10 ms. The 30 ns/'single floating-point comparison' figure is also not defensible when each evaluation computes (n/S)^(1-g), i.e. an exp/log pair. Fix: either report a measured allocation time at the claimed scale, or describe the priority-queue/lazy-greedy implementation that would actually make the outer loop O(log L) per step.

[P11 - the optimized objective is never shown to be the quantity being claimed] Q = C * F * w sums a unitless product of an attention-mass fraction, a cosine similarity, and a hand-set sigmoid across layers. Nothing in the paper establishes that sum_l Q correlates with PPL or any end metric; layer-wise KV error compounds through the residual stream rather than adding across layers, so additivity is an unexamined modelling choice, and w_l is a function of depth alone rather than of any measured sensitivity. Section 3.5 is titled 'Theoretical Properties' but contains no theorem, no bound and no proof -- it names MCKP, correctly disclaims the (1-1/e) bound, cites an FPTAS it does not use, and then offers greedy with no guarantee. The one quantitative claim in it, 'greedy achieves 118-119% of [truncated]', is impossible to interpret: for a maximization no heuristic exceeds 100% of the optimum, so the referent is either not the optimum or the number is wrong. Fix: retitle the section, define the 118-119% referent, and add a scatter of predicted Q against measured PPL across allocations -- that plot is the paper's missing keystone.

[P12 - credit assignment inverted] The abstract orders the contributions as (1) joint (n_l,b_l) allocation, (2) inverted importance, (3) mean-fill. Measured marginal effect runs the other way. The joint allocator's own isolating experiment (A1) shows it tying quant-only at 3x and losing by 3.2x/44x at 6x. The precision-set ablation (A3) shows {4,16} vs {4,8,16} differing by 0.01 in one of four cells -- i.e. the INT8 level, a third of the claimed action space, has no measurable effect. Mean-fill and inverted importance carry all the measured gain (45.09 -> 1.13 and 45.09 -> 2.52 respectively on Llama-2-7B at 6x), and both are one-line heuristics rather than the joint optimization the title promises. Additionally, contribution (4) claims 17 reimplemented baselines but only 7 ever appear in any table -- a claimed contribution with no reported data. Fix: demote the allocator claim to match its measured effect, drop or justify the INT8 level, and publish all 17 baseline rows.

[P10 - desk-reject risks] (a) The submitted source does not compile as given: '\begin{table[t]' (importance ablation), an unclosed '\section{Analysis' brace, and an unclosed '\textbf{Downstream accuracy.' brace that swallows the Limitations section heading -- the paper has limitations content but no Limitations header, which the NeurIPS checklist asks for. (b) The 18-column main results table is set \small with \tabcolsep=2pt and then wrapped in \resizebox{\textwidth}{!}{...}, which shrinks the font well below the template size; the handbook explicitly names 'decreasing margins or font sizes' as grounds for desk rejection. (c) Phrases such as 'the official artifacts were not public at submission time', 'we will update against their official code at camera-ready', 'For the camera-ready we will regenerate Table X', and the 'Caveat on baselines' block read as responses to a prior review round embedded in the manuscript; under double-blind this is a prior-report-identity risk and should be removed. (d) The checklist is \input but not visible in the provided text, so the mandatory NeurIPS LLM-usage item could not be verified, and no LLM-usage statement appears anywhere in the body.

[P8/P9 - the mechanism evidence is on a model that appears in no result] The motivating measurement in the introduction (Gini 0.43-0.93, 'a 2.1x spread'), the complementarity claim (Pearson rho = 0.194), and two of the paper's three figures (allocation_heatmap.pdf, signal_curves.pdf) are all on TinyLlama-1.1B -- a model that appears in no results table and is outside the paper's stated 7B-72B scope. The entire mechanistic case for the method therefore rests on a model whose behaviour is never connected to any reported outcome. Fix: regenerate the Gini spread, the rho, and both figures on Mistral-7B and Qwen2.5-14B.

[P6/P7 - the motivating gap is falsified by the paper's own related work] Section 1 asserts 'Nearly all existing methods apply their strategy uniformly across layers -- every layer drops the same fraction of tokens or uses the same bit-width'. Section 2, one page later, lists PyramidKV ('varies budget by layer depth'), D2O ('per-layer diversity-based allocation'), SqueezeAttention ('classifies layers'), CAKE, EvolKV, LAVa, KVTuner ('assigns per-layer mixed-precision'), KVmix and MoE-nD -- nine per-layer methods. The paper's stated gap does not exist as stated; the actual gap is narrower (online + joint over both axes) and should be claimed as such.
questions: Which value of Delta F(4->8) does the released allocator actually use -- the 0.0035 in Section 3.5 or the 0.0224 implied by your own Per-Model Fidelity Calibration table? If it is 0.0035, every allocation in the paper under-prices bit upgrades by 6.4x relative to your calibration; please rerun the main table with the corrected constant and report whether the 'quantize first' behaviour survives.

Is compression applied query-aware (question visible to the scorer) or query-agnostic (context compressed, then question appended) in your MMLU, NIAH, LongBench and GSM8K pipelines? Please state it per table. This is the single most likely explanation for SnapKV landing at 27.1-33.4% MMLU (at or below the 25% chance floor), and until it is resolved the 'ranks 1st among 17 baselines' claim cannot be evaluated.

Please give one operating point -- any model, any benchmark, any CR -- where LayerBudget beats INT4 quantization (KIVI) at equal measured bytes with non-overlapping confidence intervals. Your component ablation ties at 3x and loses by 3.2x/44x at 6x; your memory table has KIVI at 9,990 KB / 1.01 vs LayerBudget at 12,939 KB / 1.07; MMLU, LongBench, 32K PPL and all three 72B metrics are ties or losses. If the answer is 'NIAH on Llama-2-7B', note that 100 vs 93.3 on 30 cells is a 2-question difference.

Your LongBench table reports Full KV at 0.040-0.056 mean F1/ROUGE-L, roughly 500x below the published scale for these models. What is the scoring path, and does the 'matches Full KV' conclusion survive a fixed harness? Relatedly, why is LongBench-v1 used at all rather than LongBench-v2, given v1's known saturation?

The Byte-CR Reconciliation appendix claims every method's effective CR matches nominal within +/-0.05 across 1,779 checkpoints, but your CR=2x memory table reports effective 1.32x / 3.50x / 1.76x. Which audit is correct, and what is the effective byte-CR for each cell of the main results table?

Given that STAR-KV (ICML 2026), KVTC (ICLR 2026), ThinKV and MoE-nD operate at 14-20x compression or <5% cache retention, why should this community publish a method whose envelope is 2-4x and which degrades to 1.25-1.56 at 6x? What specifically prevents the greedy allocator from reaching the 10x+ regime -- the coverage power law, the INT4 floor, or the additive objective?

You state that end-to-end results on Llama-2-13B, Qwen2.5-14B and Qwen2.5-72B use the inverted-importance default 'for consistency', despite your own LOO probe showing 13B is late-bottleneck and 14B is flat. What are those tables under the per-architecture direction you recommend for deployment? The 1.56 at 6x on Llama-2-13B is presumably the visible cost of this choice.

probe_answers.answer: Alternatives that plausibly address 'reduce KV bytes per layer under a global budget': (1) Pure INT4/INT2 KV quantization -- KIVI. COMPARED head-to-head, and it wins or ties nearly everywhere (see P4/weakness 1). (2) Attention-sink + recent-window retention -- StreamingLLM. COMPARED; it loses, which is the expected outcome and is fine. (3) Heavy-hitter eviction -- H2O / SnapKV. COMPARED, but SnapKV lands at chance on MMLU, so the comparison is not usable as configured. (4) Per-layer offline mixed-precision -- KVTuner. Listed in the 17 and in the positioning table, but no numbers appear anywhere in the paper except one memory-table row (9,990 KB / 1.01, i.e. it ties KIVI and beats LayerBudget). (5) Concurrent per-layer joint (eviction, b_K, b_V) -- MoE-nD. COMPARED via reimplementation; LayerBudget loses at 6x on Mistral (1.25 vs 1.04), conceded in Limitation (5). (6) Cross-layer low-rank -- xKV. COMPARED via reimplementation; LayerBudget wins, but at 1024 tokens, which the paper itself notes is outside xKV's claimed 16K-65K regime, so the win is against a deliberately unfavourable operating point. IGNORED ENTIRELY, and these are the damaging ones: RDKV (rate-distortion bit allocation that treats eviction and quantization as endpoints of one bit-allocation scheme -- literally this paper's thesis, with a Lagrangian/water-filling solver and a fused packed-decode kernel, reporting 97.81% of full-cache LongBench accuracy at 2.48% retention and 4.5x decode speedup at 128K); HqeKV (ACL 2026 Findings, hybrid quantization+eviction with a per-element action selector, public code, 40.53 -> 49.98 under matched memory); ThinKV (hybrid quantization+eviction, near-lossless at <5% cache, 5.8x throughput); STAR-KV (ICML 2026 Spotlight, 20x with low-rank-aware mixed precision); KVTC (ICLR 2026, 20-40x under a global bit budget); DefensiveKV / Layer-DefensiveKV (ICLR 2026, per-layer allocation, RULER 91.4 at 20% cache); TurboQuant (ICLR 2026); PolyKV; ARKV; LKV; KVCompose. RDKV and HqeKV in particular occupy the paper's exact problem statement with stronger results and, for HqeKV, public code -- ignoring them is a fatal omission for a paper whose novelty claim is 'no prior online, training-free method jointly optimizes per-layer (n_l, b_l)'. Also ignored as a system alternative: NVIDIA KVPress, the de-facto harness with 30+ methods and built-in PerLayerCompressionPress and QuantizedCache, which would have removed the reimplementation risk that now undermines the SnapKV and LongBench rows.

(1) g_l -- used in the coverage equation in Section 3.2 but not defined until Section 3.3; and 'Gini coefficient of an attention row' is an economics inequality index imported without argument that a Lorenz-curve statistic is the right sparsity functional here (entropy is this field's default, and CAKE is cited as using entropy). (2) The '118-119%' figure -- appears twice (Contribution 1 and Section 3.5) with the referent truncated/absent; percent-of-what is never stated, and for a maximization a heuristic cannot exceed 100% of the optimum, so the number is uninterpretable as written. (3) B_used -- appears in the WHILE condition of Algorithm 1 and is never defined. (4) n_min = 'sink + recent' -- neither the sink count nor the recent-window size is given anywhere, so the algorithm is not reproducible; likewise the bit-upgrade step size is never stated (Delta n = 8 is given for tokens only). (5) n_h and d in the xKV appendix caption versus H and d in Section 1 -- the same quantity under two symbols, never reconciled. (6) 'CR' -- overloaded across nominal token-count CR, method-byte CR, allocator-side CR and runtime mean_memory_bytes CR; the paper acknowledges this and then still uses the bare token in captions. (7) Q(l, n_l, b_l), called 'quality' -- a unitless product of a probability mass, a cosine similarity and a sigmoid, summed across layers; the sense in which the sum is a 'quality' is never defined, and it is never measured. (8) 'Cat.', 'Ph', 'Qt', 'Jt' -- main-table row-category abbreviations, never expanded. (9) k = 5 and tau = 0.3 in the importance sigmoid -- introduced as 'steepness' and 'midpoint' with no derivation, no sensitivity study, and no statement of what tuning set produced them. (10) 'mean-fill', 'inverted importance', 'coverage law', 'the MoE-nD framing', 'allocator-side accounting' -- the paper's own coinages, used as if established terminology; a PC member would have to look each up.

Three recomputations, all from the paper's own inputs; two fail. (A) FIDELITY CONSTANT -- FAILS. Section 3.5 states Delta F(4->8) = 0.0035. From the Per-Model Fidelity Calibration table: mean F(4) = (0.9794 + 0.9758 + 0.9817 + 0.9683 + 0.9781 + 0.9810)/6 = 5.8643/6 = 0.97738; mean F(8) = (0.9998+0.9997+0.9999+0.9997+0.9998+0.9999)/6 = 0.99980. Delta F(4->8) = 0.99980 - 0.97738 = 0.02242, which is 6.4x the stated 0.0035. Delta F(8->16) = 1.0000 - 0.99980 = 0.00020, twice the stated 0.0001. Section 3.2 independently calls the F(4) gap '~2%', consistent with 0.0224 and inconsistent with 0.0035. The concavity inequality still holds, but this constant is the numerator of the bit-upgrade marginal gain, so a 6.4x error in it directly changes the allocator's action ordering. (B) MEMORY TABLE -- FAILS. Llama-3.1-8B and Mistral-7B both have 32 layers, 8 KV heads, d = 128. FP16 KV at S=512: 2 (K,V) * 32 * 512 * 8 * 128 * 2 bytes = 67,108,864 B = 67.1 MB, identical for both. The table reports Base KV = 189 MB (Llama-3.1) and 95 MB (Mistral) -- a factor of 1.989 apart for identical geometry, and neither equal to 67.1 MB -- while reporting the same 54 MB compressed size for both. The savings then follow mechanically: 1 - 54/189 = 71.4% (paper 71.2%) and 1 - 54/95 = 43.2% (paper 42.9%). So the advertised '43-72% memory savings' spread is entirely an artifact of the inconsistent Base KV; corrected, both models give ~43%. Also 1 - 218/287 = 24.0% (paper 24.3%) for Llama-2-7B. None of the three is the 50% that the table's own 'CR=2x' caption requires; effective CRs are 287/218 = 1.32x, 189/54 = 3.50x, 95/54 = 1.76x. (C) ALLOCATOR COST -- INTERNALLY CONSISTENT BUT UNDERSTATED BY ~160x. 80 * 32768/8 = 327,680 outer iterations (checks out); 327,680 * 30 ns = 9.83 ms ~ the claimed '~10 ms' (checks out). But Algorithm 1's WHILE body loops over every layer and both actions, so the real count is 327,680 * 80 * 2 = 52,428,800 marginal-gain evaluations = ~1.57 s at 30 ns each, and 30 ns is itself optimistic for an evaluation containing (n/S)^(1-g). (D) Minor: decode-latency overheads do not follow from their own columns -- Llama-2-7B 21.1/20.6 = +2.43% (reported +2.6%) and Mistral 21.1/20.4 = +3.43% (reported +3.9%), while the other three rows (+2.8%, +4.5%, +12.2%) do check out.

The abstract's most quotable number is dishonest by selection, not by fabrication. 'At 32K context on Mistral-7B, H2O at 4x collapses (83x PPL) while LayerBudget maintains 1.009x' compares against the baseline that fails, while the same table shows KIVI at 1.008 -- i.e. the strongest baseline marginally BEATS LayerBudget at that exact operating point. The honest sentence is 'ties INT4 quantization at 32K'. Likewise 'ranks first among token-compression methods' is a scope construction that removes KIVI, the only baseline that beats the method. Two baseline configurations are actively suspect. SnapKV at 27.1 / 29.6 / 29.4 / 33.4 MMLU is at or below the 25% chance floor on three models -- not a plausible result for SnapKV at these ratios, and the paper verifies only H2O against an official implementation, not SnapKV. The likely cause (query-agnostic compression order, which the paper never states) is a known ranking-flipping confound in this literature. Separately, the xKV head-to-head is run at 1024 tokens while the paper's own text concedes 'xKV's gains in their paper come from the long-context (16K-65K) regime' -- so the claim that LayerBudget 'dominates xKV at every CR' is a win at an operating point chosen to disadvantage the baseline, and the paper says so in the same sentence. Finally, the headline quality envelope is measured under mean-fill while the paper calls zero-fill 'the practical deployment setting' -- so the favourable configuration is the non-deployment one.

Nine internal contradictions. (1) Abstract 'PPL ratio <=1.03 at 4x on seven models from 7B to 72B' vs large-model table Llama-2-13B = 1.11 at 4x; the abstract's own next clause excludes that model, so the sentence contradicts itself. (2) Section 4.3 'Under zero-fill ... <=1.04 at 2-4x on all tested models' vs the zero-fill appendix table showing Llama-2-7B = 1.17 at 4x. (3) Appendix E 'every method's effective CR ... matches its nominal CR within +/-0.05' vs the CR=2x memory table's effective 1.32x / 3.50x / 1.76x (deviations 0.68, 1.50, 0.24). (4) Llama-2-7B at 6x is 1.099 in the head-to-head table and 1.17 in the main table, both stated as seq=1024 + mean-fill; and 1.13 in the Analysis section text. Three values for one cell. (5) KIVI on Llama-2-7B is 1.006 in the head-to-head table and 1.02 in the main table. (6) Section 3.5 Delta F(4->8) = 0.0035 vs 0.0224 computed from the calibration appendix and '~2%' in Section 3.2. (7) The component-analysis caption says 'The joint approach exceeds quant-only at 3x' while its own table shows exact ties (1.00 vs 1.00; 1.02 vs 1.02). (8) The importance-ablation caption asserts the universal 'Inverted importance dominates because early layers are most damaged by eviction' while Sections 3.2 and 5 state the direction reverses on Llama-2-13B and vanishes on Qwen2.5-14B. (9) Section 1 'Nearly all existing methods apply their strategy uniformly across layers' vs Section 2, which lists nine per-layer methods (PyramidKV, D2O, SqueezeAttention, CAKE, Ada-KV, EvolKV, LAVa, KVTuner, KVmix) plus MoE-nD.

The prose does not read as fabricated -- the numbers are too specific, too mutually constraining, and too often unflattering to be generated. It reads as ACCRETED: a manuscript grown by pasting rebuttal responses into whatever section was nearest. Specific evidence: the MoE-nD passage in Related Work is a single ~350-word paragraph that narrates a full head-to-head result table, concedes a loss, introduces a new method variant (LayerBudget-KV), and then appends a labelled 'Caveat on baselines:' block ending 'we will update against their official code at camera-ready' -- that is a reviewer response, not related work. Limitation (5) is the same genre. Appendix E ('Byte-CR Reconciliation') is an erratum reconciling two of the paper's own denominators and closes with 'For the camera-ready we will regenerate Table X', which presumes acceptance. Defensive reframings appear verbatim: 'The two design points are therefore best read as complementary operating regimes of the same framework rather than two competing solvers' and 'the 2x inflation in the table below is allocator overhead, not a CR-denominator inconsistency between methods'. Stylistically, almost every paragraph in Sections 3-5 opens with a bolded run-in assertion followed by one supporting number, giving the uniform rhythm the probe asks about, and Section 3.5 is titled 'Theoretical Properties' while containing no theorem -- description in place of argument. Net: not machine-generated, but the organization has been destroyed by successive patching, which is itself a presentation defect a PC will notice.

(a) OVER-ASSERTION. 'Nearly all existing methods apply their strategy uniformly across layers' -- falsified by the paper's own Section 2. 'LayerBudget ranks 1st among all token-compression methods' -- stated as a universal but supported at 1024 tokens, on 4 models, against 7 of the 17 baselines. 'These results validate the Gini stability finding ... attention sparsity profiles calibrated at short context transfer to 32K tokens without recalibration' -- asserted from PPL agreement; no Gini measurement at 32K is shown. 'Inverted importance dominates because early layers are most damaged by eviction' -- a causal universal the paper elsewhere restricts to Mistral. 'GQA models are more robust ... because shared KV heads provide natural redundancy' -- a mechanism asserted, never tested. (b) VAGUE REFERENT. 'These results validate the Gini stability finding' -- 'these results' are PPL ratios, which measure no Gini quantity. 'This is the quantize first regime.' -- 'this' spans the whole preceding bullet. 'The reduction generalizes' -- which reduction, KL or PPL? 'it autonomously avoids eviction' -- 'it' is the joint approach, two sentences after 'the joint approach' last appeared. 'The cost-model's marginal-gain ranking is robust enough that the inverted default does not collapse' -- 'robust enough' relative to what threshold? (c) THING-VS-PROCESS. 'allocation' denotes both the plan {(n_l,b_l)} and the greedy procedure ('per allocation', 'the allocator's inner loop'). 'profiling' denotes both the runtime cost and the stored artifact ('fixed profiles (calibrated once per model)'). 'compression ratio' denotes both the requested target and the delivered outcome, which is precisely what makes the CR=2x memory table unreadable. 'importance' denotes both the sigmoid weight w_l and the measured LOO sensitivity, which is how the paper ends up asserting a direction its measurements contradict. (d) FALSE PRECISION. NIAH values 93.3 / 86.7 / 73.3 / 46.7 / 26.7 are 28, 26, 22, 14 and 8 out of 30 cells, reported to one decimal as if resolved to 0.1pp. 'a 2.1x spread' for Gini 0.43 -> 0.93: the ratio of two indices bounded on [0,1] is not an interpretable spread statistic. '118-119%' of an undefined referent. 'reduces output distortion by 96%' from one model at one CR (0.249 -> 0.009 = 96.4%). '97.5% reduction' for PPL ratio 45.09 -> 1.13 treats 0 as the floor when the floor is 1.0 (against the correct excess-over-1 baseline it is 99.7%). '60-94%' improvement, a range assembled from two cells on two models. Decode overheads '+2.6%' and '+3.9%' do not equal the +2.43% and +3.43% implied by the same table's own baseline and method columns.

Thesis, one sentence: 'Allocating a token budget and a quantization bit-width per layer, by greedy marginal gain under a byte budget and with quantization spent before eviction, gives near-lossless KV cache compression at 2-4x across 7B-72B models.' Topic sentences that map cleanly to that thesis: the two-family framing in Section 1; the complementary cost structure of eviction vs quantization; the MCKP formulation; the coverage law; the greedy allocator; the main-results 'near-lossless at 2-4x' bullet; the long-context bullet; the component analysis. Paragraphs that map to NEITHER the thesis nor their own evidence -- deletion candidates, not revision candidates: (1) The MoE-nD paragraph in Related Work. Its topic sentence is about a concurrent work's positioning, but its body is a results narration plus a new method variant plus a baseline caveat -- three different documents in one paragraph. (2) Appendix E, 'Byte-CR Reconciliation'. Its topic sentence ('This appendix reconciles two memory denominators') describes an internal bookkeeping error; it belongs in a revision, not a submission. (3) Section 3.3's 'Weak correlation enables complementary allocation' paragraph. Its evidence (rho = 0.194 on TinyLlama-1.1B) is from a model that appears in no result, and rho = 0.194 shows the signals are uncorrelated, which is not the same as showing they are jointly informative -- the paragraph's evidence does not establish its own topic sentence. (4) Section 3.5's closing paragraph on 'quantize first ... emerges naturally from the marginal gains': the topic sentence claims emergence, the evidence is a restatement of the mechanism, not a measurement. (5) Limitation (5): its topic sentence announces a ceiling, its body reports a new experiment plus a new variant plus that variant's failure -- results material misfiled as a limitation. (6) The Section 1 paragraph beginning 'The uniform assumption' has an identifiable topic sentence that Section 2 refutes -- the strongest single finding of this probe.

I received LaTeX source only, not the compiled PDF, so I could NOT inspect any figure as rendered. All three figures (ppl_scaling.pdf, allocation_heatmap.pdf, signal_curves.pdf) are therefore unverified and I flag that explicitly rather than assuming they are fine. Two defects are nonetheless visible from the source and captions. First, two of the three figures are on TinyLlama-1.1B -- the allocation heatmap ('Per-layer allocation at 2x-6x on TinyLlama') and the signal curves (rho = 0.194) -- a model that appears in no results table and lies outside the paper's stated 7B-72B scope; the paper's entire visual mechanistic argument is thus made on a model whose behaviour is never linked to any reported outcome. Second, the source as provided does not compile: '\begin{table[t]' is a malformed environment, and '\section{Analysis' and '\textbf{Downstream accuracy.' have unclosed braces (the latter swallows the Limitations heading). Whatever PDF exists was therefore not produced from this source, so I cannot certify that the rendered figures and tables correspond to the text I reviewed. Additionally, the 18-column main table is wrapped in \resizebox{\textwidth}{!}{...} on top of \small and \tabcolsep=2pt, which will render its font far below template size and, in my experience, illegibly in print.

(a) ANONYMITY: the author block is 'Anonymous Author(s)', and there is no institution, funding acknowledgement, or 'our previous work' self-citation. However, several passages disclose review-cycle state in a way that risks prior-report identification: 'the official artifacts were not public at submission time', 'we will update against their official code at camera-ready', 'For the camera-ready we will regenerate Table X using mean_memory_bytes', and an explicitly labelled 'Caveat on baselines:' block. These read as responses to an earlier review round embedded in the manuscript. The fix is deletion, not elaboration. The priority claims ('To our knowledge, no prior online, training-free method jointly optimizes per-layer (n_l, b_l)'; 'The closest concurrent work is MoE-nD, which independently arrives at the same formulation') are within normal bounds but the second is unwise given the omitted RDKV/HqeKV. (b) COMPLETENESS: '\input{checklist}' is present, so the checklist is intended to be in the PDF, but its contents were not in the text provided and I could not verify that the mandatory items -- specifically the NeurIPS LLM-usage declaration -- are answered. No LLM-usage statement appears in the body, and the paper describes 17 baseline reimplementations, which is exactly the kind of implementation work the handbook says should be described if non-standard assistance was used. Also, the Limitations content exists but has no section heading, because the preceding '\textbf{Downstream accuracy.' brace is unclosed. (c) FORMAT: two concrete desk-reject risks. First, effective font reduction -- the 18-column main results table is set \small with \tabcolsep=2pt and then \resizebox{\textwidth}{!}{}, and the handbook names 'decreasing margins or font sizes' as grounds for desk rejection. Second, the source does not compile as given ('\begin{table[t]', two unclosed braces). Page count could not be verified from source, but the main body (7 sections, 2 large tables, 3 figures, 1 ablation table) is at or over the nine-content-page limit and should be measured before submission.

(a) What the code actually computes: greedy argmax over (layer, action in {add 8 tokens, upgrade bits}) of Delta[C(l,n_l) * F(b_l) * w_l] / Delta[2*n_l*H*d*b_l/8], with C = (n_l/S)^(1-g_l), F = mean cosine similarity between FP16 and dequantized K and V over 8 calibration prompts, w_l = sigma(5*(1 - l/(L-1) - 0.3)), iterated until the byte budget is exhausted. (b) Does that equal the object the theory names? No, in three places. First, the theory calls sum_l Q a 'quality' to be maximized, but no experiment anywhere in the paper relates sum_l Q to PPL or any task metric. C is validated in isolation (MAE 3.1% against measured attention mass, on one model), F is measured, w is not measured at all -- and the product-then-sum aggregation is never justified. KV perturbations propagate multiplicatively through the residual stream, so an additive cross-layer objective is a modelling assumption, not a derivation. Second, w_l is defined as depth-only, yet the quantity it is meant to represent -- per-layer eviction sensitivity -- IS directly measured by the paper's LOO probe, which finds the opposite sign on Llama-2-13B and no signal on Qwen2.5-14B. So the implementation's importance term provably does not equal the object the method section says it represents, on 2 of the 3 architectures where it was checked, and all end-to-end results were nevertheless produced with it. Third, the constant that governs the bit-upgrade branch of the same argmax, Delta F(4->8), is stated as 0.0035 in Section 3.5 but is 0.0224 by the paper's own calibration table -- a 6.4x discrepancy in the exact quantity that makes 'quantize first, evict last' emerge. (c) Borrowed-method semantics: the paper invokes MCKP and the knapsack literature, correctly declines the (1-1/e) submodular bound (the action graph is not a matroid because the per-byte cost of a token-add depends on the current b_l), cites an FPTAS it does not use, and then supplies greedy with NO guarantee -- while keeping the section title 'Theoretical Properties'. Its one quantitative claim, 'greedy achieves 118-119% of [referent truncated]', is either a typo or a category error: a maximization heuristic cannot exceed 100% of the optimum. Nothing is proved anywhere in the paper, so gate (d) does not fire on circularity, but the section as written promises theory it does not deliver.

Claimed order (abstract/intro): C1 per-layer (n_l,b_l) joint allocation with quantize-first greedy ('118-119%'); C2 inverted importance from LOO ('60-94%' at 6x); C3 mean-fill ('96%' KL reduction); C4 controlled comparison of 17 baselines; C5 16K-32K validation; C6 72B scaling. C1 -- isolating experiment: component analysis A1. Measured marginal effect vs the trivial alternative (quantize everything to INT4): 3x Mistral 1.00 vs 1.00 (zero), 3x Llama-2 1.02 vs 1.02 (zero), 6x Mistral 3.23 vs 1.00 (joint is 3.2x WORSE), 6x Llama-2 45.09 vs 1.01 (44x WORSE). The flagship contribution has zero measured benefit where it works and a large measured penalty where it does not. Ablation A3 compounds this: {4,16} vs {4,8,16} gives 1.01/3.23/1.02/45.09 vs 1.00/3.23/1.02/45.09 -- the INT8 level, one third of the claimed action space, moves one cell by 0.01. Per this probe's own rule ('a contribution billed as primary whose isolating experiment shows a small or within-noise effect is a FATAL defect'), C1 is a fatal defect. C2 -- isolating experiment: importance-direction ablation. Effect is large but only at 6x (Mistral 3.231 -> 1.283; Llama-2 45.09 -> 2.52) and modest at 4x (1.039 -> 1.008; 1.166 -> 1.002), and it is measured only on the two models where the inverted direction happens to be correct; the paper's own LOO shows it is wrong on Llama-2-13B and null on Qwen2.5-14B. So C2's measured effect is real but not general. C3 -- isolating experiment: the Analysis section. Effect is the largest single number in the paper (Llama-2-7B 6x: 45.09 -> 1.13). But the paper's own control shows median-fill and moment-matched random-fill do equally well, so the contribution is 'do not zero-fill', a one-line change. C4 -- 17 baselines claimed; 7 ever appear in a table. The other 10 have no reported data anywhere. C6 -- at 72B, KIVI matches or beats LayerBudget on PPL (1.00 vs 1.06 at 6x), NIAH (100 vs 100) and RULER (99 vs 98 at 2x), so the scaling validation demonstrates that pure quantization scales at least as well. Ranking by measured marginal effect: C3 > C2 > C1(<=0). The abstract's ranking is C1 > C2 > C3. The credit assignment is exactly inverted, and the title names the component with the smallest measured effect.

(a) ONE SENTENCE IN THIS COMMUNITY'S VOCABULARY: 'A training-free, online heuristic that allocates per-layer KV-cache token budgets and quantization bit-widths by greedy marginal gain under a global memory constraint.' This is statable without borrowing from any adjacent field, so on the narrow linguistic test the paper is NOT mis-venued, and I say so explicitly rather than manufacturing a fit objection. (b) TERMS A PC MEMBER WOULD HAVE TO LOOK UP, all of them the authors' own coinages presented as established: 'mean-fill', 'inverted importance', 'coverage law', 'the MoE-nD framing', 'allocator-side accounting', 'byte-CR reconciliation', 'LayerBudget-KV', 'Ph/Qt/Jt'. One genuine cross-field import: the Gini coefficient, an economics inequality index, applied to an attention row with no argument for why a Lorenz-curve statistic beats entropy (which the paper's own Related Work notes CAKE uses) -- and the '2.1x spread' framing (0.93/0.43) treats a [0,1]-bounded index as if ratios of it were meaningful. (c) MECHANISMS BELONGING ELSEWHERE: the vLLM LayerBudgetBlockManager, 16-token block-boundary rounding, TPOT tables, and memory-savings tables are MLSys/ASPLOS material -- but they are also the paper's weakest-supported content (one model at 512 tokens for the vLLM port, measured speedup <1x with the footnote 'amortized at higher batch sizes / longer generation' and no batch experiment, 12.2% TPOT overhead at 14B). Conversely the MCKP framing is operations research with no theorem attached. So the systems content is too thin for MLSys (no kernel, no throughput win, no serving experiment) and the theory is too thin for a theory venue; what remains for NeurIPS/ICLR is the empirical claim, which fails on its own numbers (see P12). (d) POSITIONING AGAINST THIS VENUE'S LITERATURE: no. Every one of the 20-odd compression citations is a 2024-2026 arXiv preprint or an older classic. Not one 2026 accepted paper from this venue family on this exact problem is cited: STAR-KV (ICML'26 Spotlight, 20x), KVTC (ICLR'26, 20-40x), DefensiveKV / Layer-DefensiveKV (ICLR'26, per-layer allocation, RULER 91.4 at 20% cache), TurboQuant (ICLR'26), 'Adaptive KV-Cache Compression without Manually Setting Budget' (ICLR'26), HqeKV (ACL'26 Findings), RDKV, ThinKV. The evaluation conventions are equally out of step: WikiText-2 PPL ratio as the primary metric (this community's KIVI row in the paper's own table shows why it is uninformative), LongBench-v1 instead of v2 and with visibly broken numbers, no InfiniteBench / SCBench / HELMET, RULER in two columns of one table, no effective-bits/token, and no use of KVPress. VERDICT AND FORWARD: I would not forward this to MLSys or ASPLOS -- there is no kernel and the measured speedup is below 1x. Given that the real, defensible asset is the 17-baseline unified reimplementation under one CR denominator, I would forward it to the NeurIPS Datasets & Benchmarks track (reframed as a matched-budget audit of KV-compression methods, with all 17 baselines reported, run under KVPress, on RULER/LongBench-v2, with the query-aware/query-agnostic axis made explicit) -- that version would be a genuine service to this community. Failing that, an EMNLP/ACL Findings or an efficient-NLP workshop is the right home for the method as it stands. As a main-track method paper at this venue, the 2-4x envelope against a field operating at 14-20x, combined with being dominated by INT4 quantization in its own tables, is not competitive.

(a) EXPECTED vs PRESENT for KV-cache compression in 2026: WikiText-2 PPL -- REPORTED (primary, and this is the problem: the field has demoted it). RULER 4K-128K, 13 subtasks -- ESSENTIALLY OMITTED (two columns, one model, 4096 tokens only). LongBench-v2 -- OMITTED. LongBench-v1 -- REPORTED but broken (Full KV = 0.040-0.056 where the benchmark's normal range is 20-45). InfiniteBench -- OMITTED. SCBench (the KV-cache-centric benchmark, multi-turn shared context) -- OMITTED. HELMET -- OMITTED. NIAH -- REPORTED (30 cells, 4096 tokens). MMLU -- REPORTED (0-shot, short context, where compression is least stressed). GSM8K -- REPORTED but at 200 samples with Llama-2 Full KV = 5.5%, i.e. at the floor. Reasoning-model suite (AIME'24/'25, MATH-500, GPQA-Diamond, LiveCodeBench) -- OMITTED entirely, and this is now a major sub-field for KV compression because long-output decoding is the regime where cache size actually binds. Effective bits/token, the field's common currency alongside CR -- OMITTED. Throughput / decode speedup at long context and batch -- OMITTED (TPOT at 1024 tokens only; measured speedup <1x). Peak memory at long context -- OMITTED. Confidence intervals -- essentially OMITTED (one paired-bootstrap CI is mentioned in prose; n = 6 chunks elsewhere, and the paper waves off variance with 'all methods share the same noise profile', which is an argument about baseline variance, not about the significance of method differences). Attention-backend disclosure -- OMITTED for the short-context tables (SDPA is stated only for 16K/32K), and backend choice is known to shift RULER accuracy by more than most method gaps. Query-aware vs query-agnostic compression order -- OMITTED, and it is known to reverse rankings. (b) COULD AN OMISSION REVERSE A HEADLINE CLAIM? Yes, at least two. 'Ranks 1st among token-compression methods' is established on WikiText-2 PPL, and PPL rankings are documented not to transfer to RULER; and the unstated compression order is the most likely cause of SnapKV sitting at chance on MMLU, which directly determines the ranking. Both are fatal to the headline as stated. (c) UNMEASURED TERM IN THE PAPER'S OWN OBJECTIVE: Q = C * F * w. C is validated (MAE 3.1%, one model), F is measured, but w -- the importance weight -- is never measured against anything; the one probe that would measure it (LOO) contradicts it on 2 of 3 architectures. And Q itself, the quantity the allocator maximizes, is never plotted against, or correlated with, any evaluation metric anywhere in the paper. An unvalidated term inside the optimized objective, plus an unvalidated objective, is a defect independent of any field convention. (d) WORKLOAD REGIME MISMATCH: the claims are stated over '2-4x compression, seven models, 7B-72B', but the evidence is concentrated at 1024-token context, with long context (16K/32K) covering 2-3 models at 2 CRs, NIAH/LongBench at 4096, and 72B covered by a single table. The deployment regime KV compression exists for -- 32K-128K context under batched serving -- is essentially unmeasured, and the one system table that touches it reports speedup below 1x.
